comments.author: atk
comments.text:
The edits illustrated in the post made the writing easier to read. The fact that the author puts "an" in front of every "h<vowel>" word is a noticeable (distinctly French) quirk. This is bearable, maybe even fun. However, if the rest of the writing was littered with similar quirks, it would be difficult to get used to over the course of a post, thus it would be hard to read.

I make mistakes when I write, mistakes that I did not intend to make, and mistakes that I will struggle to spot when proof reading because I have a tendency to read what I think I wrote rather than what I actually wrote. These mistakes range in variety, from duplicated words, typos, misplaced punctuation, and clunky sentence structure, to overall issues with flow.

I would need to wait a day or so before re-reading my own work to spot the issues properly. And then it may take me another day to come up with good approaches to solving some of the bigger mistakes. Writing is an iterative process, it would take a week or maybe more to get there, by which point, due to the particulars of my attention, It's likely I will have lost the necessary drive and go do something else.

I could pay someone to help, but I write posts rarely enough as it is. I have no idea where to find someone for that, I have no idea just how expensive that would be, I have no idea how long the process would take with an editor. Even thinking about doing this makes me feel averse to writing.

I don't profit from my posts, I don't write them to get clout, I don't write them to get hired, I write them because it's a topic I am excited to tell people about, and I want to hear their opinions on in return. I also enjoy these little blips of pseudo-fame on this tiny island of the internet that I care about.

So tell me, what is wrong with me pasting my prose into an LLM and saying:

"Highlight issues with this writing, focus on the obvious and the small, the bigger the change you suggest, the less likely it is I will care, so make it count. Do not give me a rewritten version, provide a list of targetted suggestions."

And then applying a handful of the more obvious suggestions, ignoring most of the rest, and using the remaining few to re-consider the structure of some parts of the text? I am incredibly sensitive to how these things reword things to sound nothing like me, so I've never wholesale replaced things I've written with the verbatim and wholesale different output of an LLM.

This lets me take the process of cleaning up a post go from a week+, to a day or two. This in turn means I maintain the focus required to actually write something, and I can produce a piece of work I am actually happy to publish. It increases my output from 1 every 2+ years to maybe once a year.

Or, I could spam the internet with messy, half written gibberish that I've not proof read even once, and then read it a week later and get horrified and discouraged by what I've done. I'd rather do that when I comment.

comments.author: Johz
comments.text:
The fact that the author puts "an" in front of every "h<vowel>" word is a noticeable (distinctly French) quirk. This is bearable, maybe even fun. However, if the rest of the writing was littered with similar quirks, it would be difficult to get used to over the course of a post, thus it would be hard to read.


This is a particularly interesting example, because traditionally, if the first syllable was not stressed, it was considered correct to use "an" instead of "a" in those cases.  For example, "an historic event".  This isn't so common these days, but as a kid I remember hearing people speak like that on the news.

As someone who writes daily in a second language, I get both sides of this.  As a native speaker, mild quirks like this are never going to make a text genuinely difficult to read.  There is already plenty of variation in how native English speakers handle these sorts of details, so adding in a few extra oddities like using "an" or "a" incorrectly isn't going to make a serious difference.  Certainly all of the examples in the text were perfectly legible before the editing pass, even if they weren't technically correct.

On the other hand, when I'm writing German, I hate that I'm constantly making mistakes, and whenever I write anything longer or more important, I always get my wife to double-check it and feel bad about all the (completely minor) issues that she points out.  And like, I'm relatively fluent in German, I feel comfortable holding a conversation in the language, and I even wrote a sketch the other day, but there's still this feeling of wanting everything to be perfect, and knowing that I'm not doing that.

So I'm clearly a hypocrite here — on the one hand, I don't think people should worry about these sorts of details, because they rarely affect readability as much as people think.  On the other hand, I do worry about these sorts of details when I'm the one doing the writing.

comments.author: Johz
comments.text:
Also, while I generally agree with the author and do a similar thing myself, I found a couple of the examples in the text ("to split" -> "that splits", and both edits to the sentence on benchmarking) weren't just grammatical corrections, but changes to the tone and style that weren't really necessary.  For me as a native English speaker, this is one of the places where I get irritated by LLM editors.  It's not necessarily that the suggestion is better or worse, it's more that I want to choose my language myself.

As a native English speaker, I'm quite comfortable ignoring suggestions like that, because I'm confident in my own mastery of the language.  When I use an LLM to do a copyediting pass, I'm really only looking for the mistakes where what I wrote is different to what I intended to write, and everything else will mostly stay the same.  But doing the same in German feels a lot harder, because it's a lot more difficult to distinguish the mistakes from the stylistic changes.  As a result, I feel less in control of what comes out — is this my style of writing, or is this the AI's?  Is a given change increasing a text's readability, or is it taking away from my personal voice?

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
I'm in the same shoes. I'm not a native speaker. I still found it a worthwhile challenge to learn to write well; I think it helped me immensely in my career and hobbies. It's also not that complicated. For me, it boiled down to three observations:




You're not writing for yourself. Put yourself in the shoes of your reader. Understand what they know and don't know, what drives them, and how much they actually want to learn about your craft. In particular, don't assume they've read every other thing you've ever posted, want to click on every outgoing link in your article, or look up every bit of jargon you use.




The hardest thing for an author is to delete text. But a good part of what an editor does is removing unnecessary words, weird tangents, and other chaff. So, get in the habit of deleting.




Finish the article, take a lunch breach or go for a walk, and then re-read the whole thing before you publish. You'll be surprised how many issues you can catch just by spacing these tasks apart.



I'd also recommend flipping through The Economist Style Guide. You don't need to follow it religiously, but it's a good read and it will make you go "huh" here and there.

That said, I understand why not everyone sees the benefits. In the era of LLMs, your coworker / rival blogger can now effortlessly produce professionally-looking text, so maybe it's all for naught. So, if you want to use an LLM as a critic / editor, I think that's  fine. Just be aware of the limitations. In my experiments, their sycophancy gets in the way: both Gemini and ChatGPT always praise me for objectively crappy explanations or analogies while suggesting cosmetic edits that rob me of my voice... convergence toward the bland.

The problem you might run into is guilt by association: most people who use LLMs for blogging just have the tool auto-generate a slop-post from a short prompt. So if someone gets a whiff that you're relying on an LLM, they might assume you're one of the slop-mongers who are ruining the web.

comments.author: chiply
comments.text:
AI is useful outside of the narrative process.

My approach is to use LLMs when I'm researching an idea (it's simply more efficient than Google and links to sources).

Once I'm confident enough to speak to the topic, I do so literally, using Whisper to transcribe.

Then I have the LLM insert that into my blog, with explicit instructions to not alter any of the transcribed text, because preserving my own voice is mission critical.

Then I editorialize the prose manually, making any verbal-only phrasing make sense in a written context.

Finally, I prompt several LLMs to function as a panel, trying to surface anything objectionable or outright false in my post (I'm human so I make mistakes and want to be aware of them).  If anything salient is in the notes, I'll manually adjust my post.

Point is LLMs are used fortuitously, and you don't need to let their prose bleed into the text.

I can see how it could be useful as a language translation layer, especially since romantic and germanic languages are so idiomatic.

comments.author: zanlib
comments.text:
I tried something like this myself, especially on the translation front, and concluded that LLMs are woefully not up to the task. Perhaps French is easier for LLMs to handle and produce satisfactory results than Polish, but the blog posts that I translated using Claude Opus from English to Polish are just... terrible, honestly.

I suspect part of it is in the nature of how autoregressive LLMs operate. In Polish sometimes what you put at the end of the sentence can change the declension of what comes before, which is not the case in English. So if the model, in the process of generating a sentence, doesn't "know" whether it'll have a masculine or feminine subject at the end of the sentence, it will put incorrect endings on preceding words.

So at the end of the day I only have a few articles translated to Polish, because the price of a competent translator is not really justifiable for an independent blog, and I am hopeless at context switching so I can't do it myself properly without expending a lot of effort that could be better spent on original content.

This is still a local LLM (although a 35B-A3B, so on the iGPU side of consumer-local). comments.author: zanlib
comments.text:
In this article the section about the keyboard, and especially the four paragraphs starting with "In theory this works great..." (in Polish: "W teorii działa to świetnie...").

I ran it through Claude Opus without any additional prompting and the result again wasn't that great. Some of the more interesting choices that I disagree with:


Using "wpm" as the unit verbatim without explaining it.

Translating "chords" to "akordy," which is only really valid when talking about musical chords. (My choice was "zbitki," i.e. "clusters.")

Translating "common sequences of two letters" literally as "popularne sekwencje dwóch liter." The word "bigram" in English is relatively uncommon and technical, whereas the corresponding Polish word "dwuznak" is known to almost everyone because of the prevalence of orthographic bigrams in Polish it is learned as early as primary school.

"according to the classic home row method" was also translated literally "zgodnie z klasyczną metodą rzędu podstawowego (home row)." This sounds very clunky because while "home row method" is recognised as a term among English typists, I'm not aware of this being the case in Polish, and there is no direct recognised equivalent of "home row" in Polish. My choice here was "zgodnie z klasyczną szkołą pisania bezwzrokowego" ("according to the classic school of touch typing").

"That takes a long time, so fast typists use a technique called 'alternative fingering'" was rendered as "Zajmuje to dużo czasu, więc szybcy maszyniści stosują technikę zwaną «alternatywnym palcowaniem»." Two choices that I would consider wrong here. Firstly, the term "maszynist(k)a" for "typist" is very dated, having fallen out of use when typist stopped being a profession (it is also a homonym, "maszynista" also means "train engine driver"). The sentence flows in English, but in Polish had to be rewritten entirely. Secondly, "alternatywne palcowanie" sounds horrible, but I couldn't find a better Polish alternative so left it as an English term in scare quotes.

"There have been some attempts" as "Podejmowano pewne próby," the word "pewne" is entirely unnecessary in the Polish translation.

"for typists that use the home row method" again as "u maszynistów korzystających z metody rzędu podstawowego" - this is a good example where the DeepL style interface would be quite a lot better, because if I had specified earlier that I don't like this word choice it would most likely not generate this sentence at all in this form after the change was made once already. (My choice: "dla osób piszących na klawiaturze metodą klasyczną").

"struggling" as "męczarni" - much too strong of a word here, "męczarnia" is more like "torture," I went with "zmagań."

"I sold the Cheapino on Facebook Marketplace" - this was an interesting point of localisation, because I hadn't actually sold it on Facebook Marketplace, but on OLX. However, OLX is likely entirely unknown in the US and UK, where these kinds of sales happen on platforms like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, so instead of relating the name of the platform exactly (which was frankly irrelevant to the discussion) and adding a margin note explaining to the international audience what it is, I used the platform that's most likely to be known to users worldwide. In the Polish version I stuck to the actual events and mentioned selling it on OLX.

"row stagger, split and arrow keys" as "przesunięcia rzędowego, klawiatury dzielonej i klawiszy strzałek" - an accurate literal translation, but my own choice was a bit different. I avoided "row stagger" up to this point, generally speaking around it descriptively, so I chose "rozłożenia wierszy." "Split" on the other hand works perfectly as an anglicism (we usually adopt anglicisms when they fit Polish phonetics and "split" is pronounced almost exactly the same in English as in Polish), so I never used the term "klawiatura dzielona," instead opting for "klawiatura split."

"It came in barebones for quite cheap" as "Przyszła w wersji barebones, dość tanio." Apart from not matching the gender (the previous sentence refers to a "model" which is masculine, whereas here the verb is conjugated for a feminine noun, I suppose "klawiatura"/"keyboard"), the word "barebones" is unlikely to be understood as a technical term for anyone not into keyboards, so I chose to also add an explanation of what this means: "Był dostępny w wersji “barebones”, bez przełączników i klawiszy za dość niską cenę."


So, you know. That's quite a lot of issues in four paragraphs of content. The problem is that if I went into this blind and just took the output and converted individual parts, it's quite likely the overall quality of the translation would be much lower, because there wouldn't be the thinking involved around how to structure the entire essay, which terms to translate, which terms to leave as anglicisms, and which to speak around.
